colors = {0.95: '#2a78d6', 0.99: '#eb6834'}                            # categorical slots 1 and 2
x = np.arange(len(TAUS))
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8), sharex=True)
for target, color in colors.items():
    met = np.array([sweep[target, t]['met'] for t in TAUS])
    reached = np.array([100 * sweep[target, t]['reached'] for t in TAUS])
    power = np.array([sweep[target, t]['power'] for t in TAUS])
    for ax, y in ((ax1, reached), (ax2, power)):
        ax.plot(x, y, '-', color=color, lw=2, label=f'target {100 * target:.0f}%')
        ax.plot(x[met], y[met], 'o', color=color, ms=8)                        # filled: met on calibration
        ax.plot(x[~met], y[~met], 'o', ms=8, mfc='white', mec=color, mew=2)  # hollow: not met
    ax1.axhline(100 * target, color=color, lw=0.8, ls=':')
    ax2.annotate(f'{100 * target:.0f}%', (x[-1], power[-1]), xytext=(6, 0), textcoords='offset points', va='center', fontsize=9)
ax1.set(ylabel='servable transmissions reaching Γ (%)', xlabel='τ (dB)', title='Reliability on unseen layouts')
ax2.set(ylabel='power, × perfect CSI', xlabel='τ (dB)', title='Power on unseen layouts', ylim=(0, None))
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.set_xticks(x, [label(t) for t in TAUS])
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
    for side in ('top', 'right'):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax1.legend(frameon=False, loc='lower right', title='hollow: target missed on calibration', title_fontsize=8, fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








The cheapest (κ, τ) per target on the calibration layouts, then the same pairs through the network on the unseen layouts, to check the analysis:

def tuned(target):
    "The (τ, sweep entry) reaching `target` on the calibration layouts with the least power there."
    ok = [tau for tau in TAUS if sweep[target, tau]['met']]
    tau = min(ok, key=lambda t: sweep[target, t]['cal_power'])
    return tau, sweep[target, tau]

checks = {}
for target in (0.95, 0.99):
    tau, s = tuned(target)
    control = lambda lay, table, m=s['margin']: LearnedChannelInversion(model, lay, table, lambda: headings, SNR_TARGET_DB, m, MAX_POWER_W)
    checks[target] = (tau, s, summary(*run(control, tau)))
print(f"{'':30s}{'reach Γ':>9s}{'power':>9s}{'withheld':>10s}{'garbled':>9s}")
for target, (tau, s, net) in checks.items():
    head = f"{100 * target:.0f}%: κ = {s['margin']:g} dB, τ = {label(tau)}"
    print(f"{head:30s}")
    for name, r in (('  analysis', s), ('  network', net)):
        print(f"{name:30s}{100 * r['reached']:8.1f}%{r['power']:8.2f}×{100 * r['withheld']:9.1f}%{100 * r['garbled']:8.1f}%")

                                reach Γ    power  withheld  garbled
95%: κ = 0.5 dB, τ = 6        
  analysis                        94.4%    2.01×      7.2%     6.8%
  network                         94.4%    2.01×      7.2%     6.8%
99%: κ = 7.75 dB, τ = ∞       
  analysis                        99.0%    6.79×      0.0%    72.0%
  network                         99.0%    6.79×      0.0%    71.3%



δ (τ = 0) is the cheapest rule, and caps the reliability. With its own margin (0.5 dB), it reaches 92% of the servable transmissions at 1.3× perfect CSI’s power, whatever the target. More margin only withholds more. (In the table above, δ had best effort’s 7.75 dB margin, and reached 88%.) Up to τ = 4 dB, neither target is reached on the calibration layouts, so both curves take the most reliable margin there, and coincide.
For 95%, a threshold of about 6 dB halves best effort’s power. τ = 6 dB with a 0.5 dB margin, the cheapest pair on the calibration layouts, reaches 94.4% on the unseen ones at 2.0× perfect CSI’s power. Best effort reaches 94.9% at 4.0×. It withholds 7.2% of the transmissions, mostly the links no power could serve (6.3%).
For 99%, best effort is the cheapest. No finite τ reaches 99% on the calibration layouts: to lose only 1%, nothing can be withheld. Raising τ towards it costs more than best effort itself (8.7× at 30 dB), because the margin then has to make up for what the threshold still withholds.
The threshold also decides what arrives garbled. Without a CRC, every unservable transmission that is sent goes out at ρ_max and mostly arrives wrong. The share of unservable messages arriving garbled grows with τ, from about 5–7% up to τ = 6 dB to 72% with best effort. A CRC removes this, whatever τ is.

So δ is right if power matters more than reliability, and about 92% delivery is enough. A threshold of a few dB is the cheapest way to a target around 95%, and best effort with a CRC is the way to 99%. Which one C3-WM should use depends on how its world model copes with missing messages: that is its task success rate, which this example doesn’t measure.

assert out['perfect CSI (eq. 21)']['reached'] == 1.0 and abs(out['perfect CSI (eq. 21)']['power'] - 1) < 1e-9
assert out["C3-WM as written: Ψ, κ = 0, δ"]['reached'] < 0.5                        # the bias of a fit in |h|²
assert out['geometry + history, κ, best effort']['reached'] > 0.985                  # the margin transfers
assert out['geometry + history, κ, best effort']['reached'] > out["C3-WM's Ψ, κ, best effort"]['reached']
assert out['geometry + history, κ, δ']['withheld'] > 0.1 and out['geometry + history, κ, δ']['wrong'] < 0.01
for target, (tau, s, net) in checks.items():                                      # the analysis is the network
    assert abs(net['reached'] - s['reached']) < 0.005 and abs(net['power'] - s['power']) < 0.02 * s['power']
assert not sweep[0.99, 0.0]['met'] and sweep[0.99, math.inf]['met']               # δ can't reach 99%

title: Network
text:
source


class Network(
    nodes:List[Node], # The nodes
    topology:Topology, # Who can communicate with whom
    protocol:Protocol, # When messages are transmitted
    backend:CommunicationBackend, # How a step's transmissions are simulated
    metrics:MetricsCollector | None=None, # What communication costs; None: a new collector
    delayed_delivery:bool=False, # Deliver a message at its transmission's start + latency (False: in the step it is sent)
):
What nodes send and receive through: the topology, protocol, backend and metrics together.

title: Network
text:
Time
The network has a clock, time. step(dt) moves it by dt, and step_to(time) moves it to a given time. Each move ends with a round: the protocol’s transmissions at that time, simulated together by the backend.

Sending: send(message) hands a message to the protocol for the next round. send(message, at=t) sends it at time t. When the clock passes t, there is a round at exactly t. This lets an application send at any time, e.g. a reply as soon as a request has arrived and been processed.
Receiving: by default, a message reaches its receiver in the round it is transmitted. With delayed_delivery=True, it arrives at its transmission’s start + latency (e.g. the airtime of its packets and their retries). receive then returns only what has arrived by the network’s time, and in_flight counts the rest. Delivered messages carry their arrival time in metadata['received_at'].

With slotted protocols (e.g. TDMAProtocol), every round is a slot, including the rounds of messages sent at a time.


source

Network.send
def send(
    message:Message, # The message
    at:float | None=None, # When it is sent (None: with the next step); not before the network's time
)->None:
Hand a message to the protocol, now or at time at.

title: Network
text:
Broadcast
broadcast(sender, payload) sends a payload to the sender’s neighbours in the topology, and to no other node. It is one message per neighbour, all tagged with the same metadata['broadcast'] id. Each neighbour hears it through its own channel, so some can get it and others not. A protocol that retransmits (e.g. max_retries) resends only to the neighbours that lost it.
The copies are one emission on the air. A power control gives them one power (see PowerControl), InterferenceBackend counts the sender’s power once, and the metrics charge the copies sent in the same round as one transmission of bits and energy (see MetricsCollector).


source

Network.broadcast
def broadcast(
    sender:str, # The sending node
    payload:Any, # What every neighbour gets
    at:float | None=None, # When it is sent (None: with the next step); see `send`
    **fields
)->List[Message]: # Other `Message` fields, e.g. `type`, `size_bits`, `metadata`
Send payload to the neighbours of sender (in the topology) only: one message each, of one broadcast.




source

Network.step_to
def step_to(
    time:float, # The new time (not before the network's time)
)->List[TransmissionResult]:
Move the clock to time: messages sent for earlier times go out at their times, then the step’s transmissions.




source

Network.receive
def receive(
    node_id:str, # The receiving node
)->List[Message]:
The messages that have reached node_id by now, in the order they arrived.



Tests

from comm_core.channel import AWGNChannel, Channel, IdentityChannel
from comm_core.backend import AnalyticalBackend
from comm_core.core import Message, TransmissionResult
from comm_core.protocol import IdealProtocol
from comm_core.topology import FullMeshTopology, StarTopology


nodes = [Node(n) for n in ('a', 'b', 'c')]
net = Network(nodes, FullMeshTopology(['a', 'b', 'c']), IdealProtocol(), AnalyticalBackend(IdentityChannel()))
net.send(Message('a', 'b', payload=[1, 2], size_bits=64))
net.send(Message('c', 'b', payload=[3], size_bits=32))
results = net.step()
assert [r.success for r in results] == [True, True] and net.receive('b')[1].payload == [3]
assert net.receive('b') == [] and net.metrics.summary().bits_received == 96
# the receiver gets what the channel delivered
class Flip(Channel):
    def transmit(self, transmission, link):
        return TransmissionResult(success=True, transmission=transmission, payload=-transmission.message.payload)
net = Network(nodes, FullMeshTopology(['a', 'b', 'c']), IdealProtocol(), AnalyticalBackend(Flip()))
net.send(Message('a', 'c', payload=5))
net.step()
assert net.receive('c')[0].payload == -5
# reset: a new episode, replayed with the same seed
def episode(net, seed):
    net.reset(seed)
    out = []
    for _ in range(20):
        net.send(Message('a', 'b', payload=0))
        out += [r.success for r in net.step()]
    return out
net = Network(nodes, FullMeshTopology(['a', 'b', 'c']), IdealProtocol(), AnalyticalBackend(AWGNChannel(5, 0.5)))
first = episode(net, 0)
assert episode(net, 0) == first and net.time == 20.0 and net.metrics.summary().transmissions == 20
# messages need a link
net = Network(nodes, StarTopology('a', ['a', 'b', 'c']), IdealProtocol(), AnalyticalBackend(IdentityChannel()))
try:
    net.send(Message('b', 'c', payload=0)); raise AssertionError('no error')
except ValueError as e:
    assert 'No link' in str(e)

Delayed delivery and messages sent at given times:

from comm_core.protocol import TDMAProtocol


class Slow(Channel):
    "Everything arrives, 0.25 time units after it is sent."
    def transmit(self, transmission, link):
        return TransmissionResult(success=True, transmission=transmission, payload=transmission.message.payload, latency=0.25)

net = Network(nodes, FullMeshTopology(['a', 'b', 'c']), IdealProtocol(), AnalyticalBackend(Slow()), delayed_delivery=True)
net.send(Message('a', 'b', payload='hi'))
net.step(dt=0.1)                                   # transmitted at 0.1, arrives at 0.35
assert net.receive('b') == [] and net.in_flight == 1
net.step(dt=0.1)
assert net.receive('b') == []
net.step(dt=0.2)                                   # 0.4
m, = net.receive('b')
assert m.payload == 'hi' and abs(m.metadata['received_at'] - 0.35) < 1e-12 and net.in_flight == 0
# sent at given times: a round at each of them, in order
net.send(Message('b', 'c', payload=2), at=0.55)
net.send(Message('a', 'c', payload=1), at=0.45)
results = net.step_to(0.6)
assert [(r.transmission.start_time, r.transmission.message.payload) for r in results] == [(0.45, 1), (0.55, 2)]
assert [m.payload for m in net.receive('c')] == []            # arrive at 0.7 and 0.8
net.step_to(0.75)
assert [m.payload for m in net.receive('c')] == [1]
try:
    net.send(Message('a', 'b', payload=0), at=0.1); raise AssertionError('no error')
except ValueError:
    pass
try:
    net.step_to(0.5); raise AssertionError('no error')
except ValueError:
    pass
# a message sent for the very time of a step goes out in that step's round (one round, one slot)
tdma = TDMAProtocol(['a'])
net = Network(nodes, FullMeshTopology(['a', 'b', 'c']), tdma, AnalyticalBackend(IdentityChannel()))
net.send(Message('a', 'b', payload=1), at=1.0)
assert len(net.step(dt=1.0)) == 1 and tdma.slot == 1

Broadcast to the neighbours:

from comm_core.topology import GraphTopology, Link
from comm_core.protocol import SlottedALOHA


# a - b - c: a's neighbour is b alone; b's are a and c
line = GraphTopology([Link('a', 'b'), Link('b', 'a'), Link('b', 'c'), Link('c', 'b')])
net = Network(nodes, line, IdealProtocol(), AnalyticalBackend(IdentityChannel()))
sent = net.broadcast('b', payload=7, size_bits=10, type='state')
assert sorted(m.receiver for m in sent) == ['a', 'c'] and len({m.metadata['broadcast'] for m in sent}) == 1
assert len({m.id for m in sent}) == 2 and all(m.type == 'state' for m in sent)
net.broadcast('a', payload=1)
net.step()
assert [m.payload for m in net.receive('a')] == [7] and [m.payload for m in net.receive('c')] == [7]
assert [m.payload for m in net.receive('b')] == [1]
# one emission: b's broadcast costs its bits once; deliveries count per neighbour
s = net.metrics.summary()
assert (s.transmissions, s.successful, s.bits_sent, s.bits_received) == (3, 3, 10, 20)
# a node without neighbours broadcasts to no one
net = Network(nodes + [Node('d')], line, IdealProtocol(), AnalyticalBackend(IdentityChannel()))
assert net.broadcast('d', payload=0) == [] and net.step() == []
try:
    net.broadcast('z', payload=0); raise AssertionError('no error')
except ValueError:
    pass
# at a given time
net.broadcast('b', payload=3, at=1.5)
assert [r.transmission.start_time for r in net.step(dt=1.0)] == [1.5, 1.5]
# a neighbour that is not a node of the network: no copy goes out
net = Network(nodes[:2], line, IdealProtocol(), AnalyticalBackend(IdentityChannel()))
try:
    net.broadcast('b', payload=0); raise AssertionError('no error')
except ValueError as e:
    assert "['c']" in str(e)
assert net.step() == []
# copies the protocol sends in different rounds (e.g. a retry) are emissions of their own
class LoseToC(Channel):
    def __init__(self): self.lost = 0
    def transmit(self, transmission, link):
        lose = transmission.receiver == 'c' and self.lost == 0
        self.lost += lose
        return TransmissionResult(success=not lose, transmission=transmission, payload=transmission.message.payload,
                                  size_bits=8, energy=1.0)
net = Network(nodes, line, SlottedALOHA(p=1.0, max_retries=1), AnalyticalBackend(LoseToC()))
net.broadcast('b', payload=0)
net.step(); net.step()
s = net.metrics.summary()
assert (s.transmissions, s.failed, s.bits_sent, s.total_energy) == (3, 1, 16, 2.0)
assert len(net.receive('c')) == 1

title: Backend
Backend
text:
Pipelines of blocks
PipelineBackend runs a step’s transmissions through blocks (see block). It calls them with the step’s inputs (transmission, link, sender, receiver, size_bits, group) and the constants it is given (e.g. noise_power), and makes a TransmissionResult of each row of the outputs:

Required: success. Missing optional outputs take defaults: the payload as sent if it arrived, no latency or energy, size_bits bits.
Radio: with h and power, the results get the SNR (the SINR with interference) and the metadata channel_gain_db and tx_power. Rows not active are outages (outage, nothing sent); rows with half_duplex were sent, but their receiver was transmitting.
Metadata: info (a dict per row) is added to the metadata.

The radio channels (see radio) are pipelines of this kind, so a pipeline of your own can reuse their blocks: replace one, add one, or wrap a Sionna block in Named.


source

step_inputs
def step_inputs(
    transmissions:List[Tuple[Transmission, Link]], # The transmissions of a step, with their links
)->dict:
The named inputs of a step: STEP_INPUTS, one row per transmission (see the names in block).




source

PipelineBackend
class PipelineBackend(
    blocks:Pipeline | Sequence[Block], # The blocks (checked against the step's inputs and the constants)
    **constants
):
A step’s transmissions through blocks: the step’s named inputs in, a TransmissionResult per row out.




source

to_results
def to_results(
    state:dict, # The named arrays of a step after its blocks, with its inputs
)->List[TransmissionResult]:
The TransmissionResult of each transmission, from the named outputs (see above).



from comm_core.core import Message, Node
from comm_core.network import Network
from comm_core.topology import FullMeshTopology
from comm_core.protocol import IdealProtocol


# a channel of two blocks: packets up to a size arrive, after their time on the air
class Small(Block):
    outputs = ('success',)
    def __init__(self, limit):
        self.limit = limit
    def call(self, size_bits):
        return size_bits <= self.limit

class Rate(Block):
    outputs = ('latency',)
    def call(self, size_bits, rate_bps):
        return size_bits / rate_bps

backend = PipelineBackend([Small(1000), Rate()], rate_bps=1e6)
net = Network([Node('a'), Node('b')], FullMeshTopology(['a', 'b']), IdealProtocol(), backend)
net.send(Message('a', 'b', 'x', size_bits=800)); net.send(Message('a', 'b', 'y', size_bits=5000))
r1, r2 = net.step()
assert r1.success and r1.payload == 'x' and r1.latency == 8e-4 and r1.size_bits == 800 and r1.snr_db is None
assert not r2.success and r2.payload is None and r2.metadata == {}
assert net.receive('b')[0].payload == 'x' and backend.transmit_all([]) == []
try:
    PipelineBackend([Rate()]); raise AssertionError('no error')        # rate_bps: neither an input nor a constant
except ValueError as e:
    assert 'rate_bps' in str(e)

title: System-level simulation
text:
System-level simulation in the sense of Sionna SYS: what matters is how many links work and how well, not the bits of each transmission. A PHY abstraction replaces the bits. It maps a transmission’s SNR to a packet error rate, and the packet is lost with that probability. It is fast, so it suits training and large numbers of agents. LinkLevelChannel (see link) simulates the bits instead, and gives the same packet error rates (tested there).
A system-level channel is a RadioChannel (see radio) whose receiver is a PHY abstraction (an ErrorModel, see phy_abstraction), then Decide, which draws what arrives. The other steps are blocks of their own modules, the same at both levels: h from a Fading (propagation), the power from a PowerControl (power_control), the interference and the SINR (interference), the airtime (radio). The rate of a transmission is link_adaptation’s. Which links transmit when is decided by the Protocol.

title: System-level simulation
text:
System-level channel
A transmission’s SINR gives its packet error rate (the ErrorModel), and the packet is lost with that probability. A packet that arrives is the payload as sent.

Size and timing: message.size_bits is the packet size. The timing counts the symbols the error model reports: one per bit for the simple models, the resource elements for SionnaErrorModel.
Blocks: the receiver is the ErrorModel, then Decide, which draws whether each packet arrives. transmit_batch handles several transmissions with one call of each block. The backends use it for a step’s transmissions.
Subcarriers: with a frequency-selective fading (e.g. RayTracedPathsFading with subcarriers), the error model gets the SINR at each subcarrier.



source

SystemLevelChannel
class SystemLevelChannel(
    fading:Fading | None=None, # The coefficient h of a transmission; None: h = 1
    power_control:PowerControl | None=None, # Transmit power and outages; None: the link's tx_power_w
    noise_power:float=1.0, # Noise power at the receiver
    per_model:str | ErrorModel='bpsk', # 'bpsk', 'threshold', or an `ErrorModel` (e.g. `SionnaErrorModel`)
    snr_threshold_db:float=10.0, # The 'threshold' model's SNR
    seed:int | None=None, # Seed of the packet losses and the fading
):
A PHY abstraction: SINR -> packet error rate -> the packet arrives intact or is lost. No bits are simulated.



Tests

import math

import numpy as np

from comm_core.core import Message, Transmission
from comm_core.phy_abstraction import EESMErrorModel, packet_error_rate
from comm_core.power_control import ChannelInversion, FixedPower
from comm_core.propagation import NoFading, RayleighFading
from comm_core.topology import Link


def send(ch, link=Link('a', 'b'), n=1, size_bits=100, **metadata):
    t = Transmission(message=Message('a', 'b', 'hi', size_bits=size_bits, metadata=metadata), sender='a', receiver='b', start_time=0.0)
    return [ch.transmit(t, link) for _ in range(n)]

for snr_db, delivered in ((10, 1.0), (0, 0.0)):                 # 100 bits: always through at 10 dB, never at 0 dB
    rs = send(SystemLevelChannel(noise_power=10 ** (-snr_db / 10), seed=0), n=50)
    assert np.mean([r.success for r in rs]) == delivered and abs(rs[0].snr_db - snr_db) < 1e-9
r = rs[0]
assert r.size_bits == 100 and r.energy == 100 and r.latency == 0 and r.metadata == {'channel_gain_db': 0.0, 'tx_power': 1.0}
# in between: lost as often as the packet error rate says, reproducibly
ch = SystemLevelChannel(noise_power=10 ** -0.6, seed=0)        # 6 dB, 100 bits
ch.reset(seed=3); first = [r.success for r in send(ch, n=2000)]
ch.reset(seed=3); assert [r.success for r in send(ch, n=2000)] == first
assert abs(1 - np.mean(first) - packet_error_rate(6, 100)) < 0.03
# the threshold model, channel inversion (outages), a perfect link, a finite bandwidth
assert send(SystemLevelChannel(noise_power=1.0, per_model='threshold', snr_threshold_db=-1))[0].success
for h, sent in ((1.2, True), (0.1, False)):
    r, = send(SystemLevelChannel(fading=NoFading(h), power_control=ChannelInversion(10, max_power=10)))
    assert r.success == sent and r.size_bits == (100 if sent else 0) and r.metadata.get('outage', False) != sent
r, = send(SystemLevelChannel(fading=NoFading(math.inf), noise_power=1e9))
assert r.success and r.snr_db == math.inf
r, = send(SystemLevelChannel(), link=Link('a', 'b', bandwidth_hz=1e6, tx_power_w=0.5))
assert abs(r.latency - 1e-4) < 1e-15 and abs(r.energy - 0.5e-4) < 1e-15


# a frequency-selective fading: the error model gets the SINR at each subcarrier
class TwoSubcarriers(Fading):
    def coefficient(self, transmission, link):
        return 1.0
    def response(self, transmission, link):
        return np.array([1.0, 0.1])                                      # the second subcarrier faded by 20 dB

class Recorder(ErrorModel):
    def rate(self, sinr, size_bits, group=None):
        self.sinr = sinr
        return np.zeros(len(sinr)), np.asarray(size_bits), [{'seen': True} for _ in sinr]

recorder = Recorder()
r, = send(SystemLevelChannel(fading=TwoSubcarriers(), noise_power=0.1, per_model=recorder))
assert np.allclose(recorder.sinr[0], [10.0, 0.1]) and r.metadata['seen']
assert abs(r.snr_db - 10 * np.log10(np.mean([10.0, 0.1]))) < 1e-9          # the mean SNR
# a batch: the same results as one at a time, with one call of the error model
ch1, ch2 = SystemLevelChannel(noise_power=10 ** -0.6, seed=4), SystemLevelChannel(noise_power=10 ** -0.6, seed=4)
pairs = [(Transmission(message=Message('a', 'b', k, size_bits=100), sender='a', receiver='b', start_time=0.0), Link('a', 'b')) for k in range(50)]
assert [r.success for r in ch1.transmit_batch(pairs)] == [ch2.transmit(t, l).success for t, l in pairs]
try:
    SystemLevelChannel(per_model='qam'); raise AssertionError('no error')
except ValueError:
    pass

In a Network, the topology and the protocol decide which transmissions happen, and the channel decides what arrives:

from comm_core import Network, Node, FullMeshTopology, IdealProtocol, AnalyticalBackend
from comm_core.propagation import RayleighFading


ch = SystemLevelChannel(fading=RayleighFading(), power_control=ChannelInversion(10, max_power=20), seed=0)
nodes = ['a', 'b', 'c']
net = Network([Node(n) for n in nodes], FullMeshTopology(nodes), IdealProtocol(), AnalyticalBackend(ch))
net.reset(seed=0)
for step in range(20):
    for s in nodes:
        for r in nodes:
            if s != r:
                net.send(Message(s, r, payload=step, size_bits=64))
    net.step()
m = net.metrics.summary()
assert m.transmissions == 20 * 6 and 0 < m.failed < m.transmissions        # deep fades: outages


# a broadcast: the error model gets its copies' broadcast (`group`)
class Grouped(ErrorModel):
    def rate(self, sinr, size_bits, group=None):
        self.group = group
        return np.zeros(len(sinr)), np.asarray(size_bits, int), [{} for _ in sinr]
nodes = ['a', 'b', 'c']
for model in (Grouped(), 'bpsk', 'threshold', EESMErrorModel(beta=1.0, threshold_db=0.0)):
    ch = SystemLevelChannel(per_model=model, noise_power=1e-3)
    net = Network([Node(n) for n in nodes], FullMeshTopology(nodes), IdealProtocol(), AnalyticalBackend(ch))
    sent = net.broadcast('a', payload=1, size_bits=8)
    net.send(Message('b', 'c', payload=2, size_bits=8))
    assert all(r.success for r in net.step())
groups = Grouped()
net = Network([Node(n) for n in nodes], FullMeshTopology(nodes), IdealProtocol(), AnalyticalBackend(SystemLevelChannel(per_model=groups)))
sent = net.broadcast('a', payload=1, size_bits=8)
net.send(Message('b', 'c', payload=2, size_bits=8))
net.step()
assert groups.group == [sent[0].metadata['broadcast']] * 2 + [None]
# no broadcast in the step: no `group`
net.send(Message('b', 'c', payload=2, size_bits=8)); groups.group = 'unset'; net.step()
assert groups.group is None



Its blocks
The channel is its blocks: pipeline() gives them, and a PipelineBackend (see backend) runs a pipeline of your own. Here a block of shadowing is added after the fading:

from comm_core.backend import PipelineBackend
from comm_core.block import Block
from comm_core.interference import SINR
from comm_core.radio import Airtime


ch = SystemLevelChannel(fading=RayleighFading(), noise_power=0.1, seed=0)
assert [type(b).__name__ for b in ch.pipeline()] == ['RayleighFading', 'FixedPower', 'SINR', 'BPSKErrorModel', 'Decide', 'Airtime']
assert ch.pipeline() is ch.pipeline()                                    # built once, while the blocks stay
ch.fading = NoFading(1.0)
assert type(ch.pipeline()[0]).__name__ == 'NoFading'                       # an attribute changed: a new pipeline

class Shadowing(Block):
    "A loss of `db` on every link."
    outputs = ('h',)
    def __init__(self, db):
        self.db = db
    def call(self, h):
        return h * 10 ** (-self.db / 20)

backend = PipelineBackend([NoFading(1.0), Shadowing(10.0), FixedPower(), SINR(), BPSKErrorModel(), Decide(), Airtime()],
                          noise_power=0.01)
t = Transmission(message=Message('a', 'b', 'hi', size_bits=100), sender='a', receiver='b', start_time=0.0)
r = backend.transmit(t, Link('a', 'b'))
assert abs(r.snr_db - 10) < 1e-9 and abs(r.metadata['channel_gain_db'] + 10) < 1e-9 and r.success   # 20 dB - 10 dB
# the same results as the channel, block for block
ch = SystemLevelChannel(noise_power=10 ** -0.6, seed=4)
same = PipelineBackend(ch.pipeline(), noise_power=ch.noise_power)
ch.reset(seed=4); a = [r.success for r in ch.transmit_batch([(t, Link('a', 'b'))] * 200)]
ch.reset(seed=4); b = [r.success for r in same.transmit_all([(t, Link('a', 'b'))] * 200)]
assert a == b and 0 < sum(a) < 200

title: Blocks
text:
A Block is one step of a simulation, written like a Sionna block: it takes arrays and returns arrays, its work is in call, and build sets up what depends on the inputs’ shapes, once, before the first call. A larger step is a block whose call runs smaller ones, or a Pipeline of them.
Unlike Sionna’s, a comm-core block is not a torch.nn.Module: the arrays are numpy arrays or torch tensors, and the block does not convert them. Two things are added for a network simulation:
The radio channels are made of blocks: a Fading gives h, a PowerControl the power, then the SINR, the interference, a PHY abstraction or the bits, and the airtime (see radio).
source

Block
class Block(
    *args, **kwargs
):
A processing step: arrays in, arrays out (numpy or torch). Subclasses write call, and build if they need the inputs’ shapes.
source

Block.call
def call(
    *args, **kwargs
)->Any:
The block’s work: its inputs -> its outputs (one value, a tuple in the order of outputs, or a dict by name).
source

Block.build
def build(
    *shapes, **kwshapes
)->None:
Set up what depends on the shapes of the inputs (given like call gets the inputs); runs once, before the first call.
source

Block.reset
def reset(
    seed:int | None=None, # The episode's seed; None: keep the random generators as they are
)->None:
A new episode: reseed this block, and its sub-blocks with seeds derived from seed.
A block is a class with a call. Here a fading that draws h for each link, with the number of subcarriers fixed by the first input it sees:
class Draw(Block):
    outputs = ('h',)
    def __init__(self, num_subcarriers=None):
        self.num_subcarriers = num_subcarriers
    def build(self, sender):                    # the shape of `sender`, as `call` gets it
        if self.num_subcarriers is None:
            self.num_subcarriers = 1
    def call(self, sender):
        n = (len(sender), self.num_subcarriers)
        return (self.rng.standard_normal(n) + 1j * self.rng.standard_normal(n)) / np.sqrt(2)

d = Draw()
assert not d.built and d.inputs == ('sender',) and d.required == ('sender',)
h = d(np.array(['a', 'b', 'c']))
assert d.built and h.shape == (3, 1) and d.num_subcarriers == 1
# reset(seed): the same draws again
d.reset(seed=0); first = d(np.array(['a', 'b']))
d.reset(seed=0); assert (d(np.array(['a', 'b'])) == first).all()
d.reset(); assert not (d(np.array(['a', 'b'])) == first).all()     # no seed: the generator goes on
# sub-blocks: found in attributes, lists and dicts, reset with their own seeds, updated with the block
class Pair(Block):
    def __init__(self):
        self.first, self.others = Draw(1), [Draw(1)]
        self.times = []
    def update(self, time):
        self.times.append(time)
        super().update(time)

p = Pair()
assert p.children() == [p.first, p.others[0]] and len(list(p.walk())) == 3
p.reset(seed=1)
x, y = p.first(['a']), p.others[0](['a'])
assert x != y                                                     # different seeds
p.reset(seed=1); assert p.first(['a']) == x
p.update(2.0); assert p.times == [2.0]

title: Blocks
text:
Pipeline
A Pipeline runs blocks in a row. It keeps the named arrays of a call: its inputs, then each block’s outputs. Each block gets the ones its call takes, by name, and adds its outputs; a later block can replace an array (e.g. Interference narrows active). It returns all of them, as a dict.
With inputs given, the wiring is checked when the pipeline is made: a block needing an array that is neither an input nor an earlier block’s output is an error then, not in the middle of a simulation. An input with a default in a block’s call is optional: the block gets it if it is there.
A pipeline is itself a block, so pipelines nest. When a list does not fit (branches, feedback), a block with its own call can run its sub-blocks in any order, as in Sionna.


source

Pipeline
class Pipeline(
    blocks:Sequence[Block], # The blocks, in order
    inputs:Sequence[str] | None=None, # Names the pipeline is called with; given, the wiring is checked now
):
Blocks in a row, wired by name: each gets the inputs and earlier outputs its call takes, and adds its outputs.



class Scale(Block):
    outputs = ('x',)
    def __init__(self, factor):
        self.factor = factor
    def call(self, x, offset=0.0):
        return self.factor * x + offset

class Stats(Block):
    outputs = ('mean', 'peak')
    def call(self, x):
        return x.mean(), x.max()

pipe = Pipeline([Scale(2.0), Scale(3.0), Stats()], inputs=('x',))
out = pipe(x=np.array([1.0, 2.0]))
assert out['x'].tolist() == [6.0, 12.0] and out['mean'] == 9.0 and out['peak'] == 12.0    # x replaced in turn
assert pipe.required == ('x',) and pipe.outputs == ('x', 'mean', 'peak')
assert pipe(x=np.array([1.0]), offset=1.0)['x'].tolist() == [10.0]                          # an optional input
# the wiring is checked when the pipeline is made
try:
    Pipeline([Stats()], inputs=('y',)); raise AssertionError('no error')
except ValueError as e:
    assert "Stats needs ['x']" in str(e)
# without `inputs`, the pipeline finds them; pipelines nest
inner = Pipeline([Scale(2.0), Stats()])
assert inner.inputs == ('x', 'offset') and inner.required == ('x',)
outer = Pipeline([Scale(10.0), inner], inputs=('x',))
assert outer(x=np.array([1.0]))['peak'] == 20.0
assert [type(b).__name__ for b in outer] == ['Scale', 'Pipeline'] and len(outer) == 2


# reset reaches every block, each with its own seed: the same seed, the same run
noisy = Pipeline([Draw(4), Draw(4)])
noisy.reset(seed=5); a = noisy(sender=['a'])['h']
noisy.reset(seed=5); assert (noisy(sender=['a'])['h'] == a).all()
try:
    Pipeline([lambda x: x]); raise AssertionError('no error')
except TypeError as e:
    assert 'Named' in str(e)

title: Blocks
section: Named: any callable, e.g. a Sionna block
text:
Named: any callable, e.g. a Sionna block
Named makes a block of any callable: a function, or a Sionna block, which takes and returns tensors in order. inputs names what it is given (in order, or as a dict from its keyword arguments to names), and outputs names what it returns. With numpy=True, tensors it returns become numpy arrays, for the blocks after it.
Sionna blocks convert numpy inputs to tensors themselves (on their device, at their precision), so they mix with comm-core blocks in a Pipeline.


source

Named
class Named(
    block:Callable, # A callable: a function, a Sionna block, ...
    inputs:Sequence[str] | Mapping[str, str], # Names of its arguments, in order; or {keyword argument: name}
    outputs:Sequence[str] | str, # Names of what it returns, in order
    numpy:bool=False, # Return numpy arrays instead of torch tensors
    **kwargs
):
Any callable as a block (e.g. a Sionna block): the names of its inputs and of its outputs.



# a function, by position or by keyword, with fixed arguments
power = Named(lambda h, p: p * np.abs(h) ** 2, ('h', 'power'), 'rx_power')
assert power.inputs == ('h', 'power') and power(h=np.array([2.0]), power=np.array([0.5]))[0] == 2.0
clip = Named(np.clip, {'a': 'x'}, 'x', a_min=0, a_max=1)
out = Pipeline([Scale(2.0), clip], inputs=('x',))(x=np.array([-1.0, 0.2, 3.0]))
assert out['x'].tolist() == [0.0, 0.4, 1.0]


import importlib

Sionna PHY’s blocks, composed with a comm-core block: 16-QAM over AWGN, the bits’ error rate counted by a block of ours.

AWGN = importlib.import_module('sionna.phy.channel').AWGN
mapping = importlib.import_module('sionna.phy.mapping')
BinarySource, Demapper, Mapper = mapping.BinarySource, mapping.Demapper, mapping.Mapper

class BitErrors(Block):
    outputs = ('ber',)
    def call(self, bits, llr):
        return float(((llr > 0) != (bits > 0.5)).mean())

qam = Pipeline([
    Named(BinarySource(), ('shape',), 'bits', numpy=True),
    Named(Mapper('qam', 4), ('bits',), 'x'),
    Named(AWGN(), ('x', 'no'), 'y'),
    Named(Demapper('app', 'qam', 4), ('y', 'no'), 'llr', numpy=True),
    BitErrors(),
], inputs=('shape', 'no'))
out = qam(shape=[100, 400], no=10 ** (-20 / 10))            # 20 dB
noisy = qam(shape=[100, 400], no=10 ** (-10 / 10))          # 10 dB
print(f"16-QAM bit error rate: {out['ber']:.4f} at 20 dB, {noisy['ber']:.3f} at 10 dB")
assert out['ber'] < 1e-3 < noisy['ber'] and isinstance(out['llr'], np.ndarray)

title: Blocks
text:
The names
The blocks of comm-core use these names, so that any of them works in any pipeline. For a step of a Network, PipelineBackend (see backend) gives the inputs, and turns the outputs into the results. Each array has one row per transmission, in the order of the step.








Name
Shape
What




transmission, link
list
The transmissions of the step, and their links (inputs)


sender, receiver
list
Their nodes (inputs)


size_bits
(n,)
message.size_bits, 0 if none (input)


group
list
The broadcast of each, None for a unicast (input)


noise_power
number
Noise power at the receivers (input)


h
(n, K)
Channel coefficient at each of K subcarriers (one: flat); inf: the nodes at the same place


power, active
(n,)
Transmit power, and whether the transmission is sent and received (False: an outage)


interference, half_duplex
(n,)
Power of the other senders at the receiver; whether the receiver was transmitting


sinr
(n, K)
Linear SINR at each subcarrier


per, num_symbols, info
(n,), (n,), list
A PHY abstraction’s packet error rate, symbols on the air, and metadata


success, payload
(n,), list
Whether each arrived, and what the receiver got (default: the payload as sent)


error_rate, num_bits
(n,)
The bits’ error rate, and the bits on the air (link level)


latency, energy
(n,)
Time on the air, and transmit energy

title: Levels of fidelity
text:
A 392-bit message (49 codebook indices of 8 bits) over a flat channel, at SNRs from −4 to 12 dB, at each level:



level
what it does




analytic
packet_error_rate: uncoded BPSK, independent bit errors


SystemLevelChannel
draws losses from that rate


LinkLevelChannel (with a CRC)
simulates every bit, uncoded BPSK


SionnaErrorModel
5G NR with LDPC codes, from Sionna SYS’s tables (MCS 3 and 9)


SionnaLinkChannel
every bit of 5G NR with Sionna PHY, at the same MCSs



The Sionna rows need Sionna 2 (pip install 'comm-core[sionna]'). Their cells are flagged #| sionna, and their saved output is shown.

import math

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from comm_core import *


import time

The radio levels are the same blocks up to the SINR (see radio); only the receiver differs, so the same fading and power control run at every level:

for channel in (SystemLevelChannel(), LinkLevelChannel()):
    print(f'{type(channel).__name__:20s}', ' → '.join(type(b).__name__ for b in channel.pipeline()))

SystemLevelChannel   NoFading → FixedPower → SINR → BPSKErrorModel → Decide → Airtime
LinkLevelChannel     NoFading → FixedPower → SINR → BitLevelLink → Airtime



SNRS = np.arange(-4, 12.5, 1.0)
INDICES = np.arange(49) * 5
N = 300

def pairs(n, payload=INDICES, size_bits=392):
    return [(Transmission(Message('a', 'b', payload, size_bits=size_bits), 'a', 'b', 0.0), Link('a', 'b')) for _ in range(n)]

def loss(channel, n=N):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    rs = channel.transmit_batch(pairs(n))                    # one call of each of the channel's blocks
    return 1 - np.mean([r.success for r in rs]), (time.perf_counter() - t0) / n

curves, cost = {}, {}
curves['analytic (uncoded BPSK)'] = [packet_error_rate(s, 392) for s in SNRS]
out = [loss(SystemLevelChannel(noise_power=10 ** (-s / 10), seed=0)) for s in SNRS]
curves['SystemLevelChannel'], cost['SystemLevelChannel'] = [o[0] for o in out], np.mean([o[1] for o in out])
out = [loss(LinkLevelChannel(noise_power=10 ** (-s / 10), drop_corrupted=True, seed=0)) for s in SNRS]
curves['LinkLevelChannel'], cost['LinkLevelChannel'] = [o[0] for o in out], np.mean([o[1] for o in out])


print(f'{"SionnaLinkChannel":20s}', ' → '.join(type(b).__name__ for b in SionnaLinkChannel().pipeline()))
for mcs in (3, 9):
    model = SionnaErrorModel(mcs_index=mcs)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    curves[f'SionnaErrorModel, MCS {mcs}'] = list(model([np.array([10 ** (s / 10)]) for s in SNRS], np.full(len(SNRS), 392))[0])
    cost['SionnaErrorModel'] = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(SNRS)
    out = [loss(SionnaLinkChannel(noise_power=10 ** (-s / 10), mcs_index=mcs, num_bp_iter=50, seed=0), n=150) for s in SNRS]
    curves[f'SionnaLinkChannel, MCS {mcs}'], cost['SionnaLinkChannel'] = [o[0] for o in out], np.mean([o[1] for o in out])

SionnaLinkChannel    NoFading → FixedPower → SINR → SionnaLink → Airtime



fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.5))
styles = {'analytic': ('k', '-'), 'SystemLevelChannel': ('C0', 'o'), 'LinkLevelChannel': ('C1', 's'),
          'SionnaErrorModel, MCS 3': ('C2', '-'), 'SionnaLinkChannel, MCS 3': ('C2', 'o'),
          'SionnaErrorModel, MCS 9': ('C3', '-'), 'SionnaLinkChannel, MCS 9': ('C3', 'o')}
for name, y in curves.items():
    color, style = next((v for k, v in styles.items() if name.startswith(k)), ('C4', '-'))
    y = np.maximum(np.array(y, float), 1e-3)
    if style == '-':
        ax.plot(SNRS, y, color=color, label=name)
    else:
        ax.plot(SNRS, y, style, color=color, mfc='none', label=name)
ax.set(yscale='log', ylim=(8e-4, 1.5), xlabel='SNR (dB)', ylabel='messages lost (none: drawn at 0.001)', title='392-bit messages at each level')
ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which='both'); ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc='center left', bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 0.5))
plt.tight_layout()
print('time per message:', {k: f'{1e3 * v:.3f} ms' for k, v in cost.items()})

time per message: {'SystemLevelChannel': '0.028 ms', 'LinkLevelChannel': '0.102 ms', 'SionnaErrorModel': '0.193 ms', 'SionnaLinkChannel': '5.564 ms'}










Uncoded levels agree. The system level follows the analytic rate, and the bit-level simulation follows it too (lines and markers of the same colour).
Coding moves the curves. With 5G NR’s LDPC codes, a message survives at SNRs where uncoded BPSK loses everything: MCS 3 from about −2 dB. Lower MCSs are more robust, higher ones faster. (MCS 0–2, with code rates below 1/5, are not available at the link level: Sionna’s LDPC encoder doesn’t support them.)
Sionna SYS against Sionna PHY. The tables (lines) and the bit-level simulation (markers) agree within about a dB at these MCSs. The bit level is 0.5–1 dB worse.
Cost. Each level costs more, up to several milliseconds per message (5–15 ms here) for every bit of 5G NR on a CPU. That’s why training runs at the system level and the link level is for checking.


assert np.allclose(curves['SystemLevelChannel'], curves['analytic (uncoded BPSK)'], atol=0.1)
assert np.allclose(curves['LinkLevelChannel'], curves['analytic (uncoded BPSK)'], atol=0.1)

title: Remote UAV control, built from blocks
text:
In oHJB (Shiri, Park and Bennis, Remote UAV Online Path Planning via Neural Network Based Opportunistic Control), a base station (BS) steers a UAV to a destination. In each control round k, the UAV sends its state, the BS updates its controller with it and sends back either an action (aHJB) or the controller itself (mHJB), which the UAV then runs on its own. oHJB sends actions first and switches to the controller once it has seen enough states and the link has become slow.
The communication model (Section III-A) is a chain of steps, and each one is a comm-core block (see block). Built as a PipelineBackend, each step can be replaced on its own:
The paper’s names follow the BS: the downlink (DL) is the UAV sending its state to the BS (the BS downloads it), and the uplink (UL) is the BS sending back an action or the controller (uploading it).
What is not the paper’s: the controller. The paper’s HJB NN (eqs. 7–9) is a 54-weight polynomial model trained at each received state. Its features are sixth powers of positions in metres, and the paper doesn’t say how they are scaled, so it can’t be rebuilt as written. It is replaced by the exact solution of the HJB equation for the quadratic part of the cost (eq. 1 without its first term), whose value function is quadratic: the LQR. It is reached one update per received state, which plays the same role as the paper’s training:
Three other choices aren’t the paper’s: * Acceleration limit. Accelerations are limited to 1 m/s², which gives at most 10 m/s against the drag. The paper’s Fig. 2 stays under 8 m/s. * Mission end. The mission ends when the UAV is within 2 m of the destination at under 0.5 m/s. The paper doesn’t give r_th or v_th. * Distance. The distance d in eqs. 11–12 is the 3-D distance. With d = ‖r − r_s‖, as written, it would be 0 at the start, and eq. 12’s √(d² − h²) shows d includes the altitude.
import math
from collections import deque

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import solve_continuous_are

from comm_core import *
crumbs: Remote UAV control, built from blocks

title: Remote UAV control, built from blocks
text:
Settings
As in the paper’s Section IV. Powers are in watts, and the noise power is the noise density over the bandwidth.

dBm = lambda x: 10 ** ((x - 30) / 10)
BS = np.array([150.0, 100.0])                 # the BS, and the UAV's start (r_s); the destination is the origin
ALTITUDE, FC_GHZ, W = 30.0, 2.0, 2e6          # h (m), carrier (GHz), bandwidth (Hz)
NOISE_W = dBm(-118) * W                       # N_i W
P_DL, P_UL, P_UL_MAX = dBm(20), dBm(23), dBm(26)
b, M_WEIGHTS = 80, 54                         # 10 bytes per number; the controller's weights
B_STATE, B_ACTION, B_MODEL = 4 * b, 2 * b, M_WEIGHTS * b
D_TH, ALPHA, N_AVG, DN_TH = 2.0, 0.2, 5, 50   # deadline (s), oHJB's switching rule
C0, C1, C2, C3 = 0.1, 0.015, 0.015, 0.005
V_O, V_NOISE, DT = np.array([1.0, -1.0]), 0.1, 0.1   # mean wind (m/s), its perturbation, the time step (s)
A_MAX, R_TH, V_TH = 1.0, 2.0, 0.5             # not in the paper (see above)

title: Remote UAV control, built from blocks
text:
The pipeline
The blocks in order, with the library’s SINR and Airtime between them. The topology has one link per direction, each with its bandwidth and power:

def radio(power_control, bs=BS):
    "The communication model of oHJB, as blocks."
    return [UAVPathLoss(bs, ALTITUDE, FC_GHZ), power_control, SINR(), Capacity(), Airtime(), Deadline()]

UAV_BS = Link('uav', 'bs', bandwidth_hz=W, tx_power_w=P_DL)          # the paper's downlink: the state
BS_UAV = Link('bs', 'uav', bandwidth_hz=W, tx_power_w=P_UL)          # the paper's uplink: an action or the model
TOPOLOGY = GraphTopology([UAV_BS, BS_UAV])

backend = PipelineBackend(radio(DeadlinePower(P_UL_MAX)), noise_power=NOISE_W)
print(' → '.join(type(block).__name__ for block in backend.pipeline))
print('inputs:', backend.pipeline.required)
print('outputs:', backend.pipeline.outputs)

UAVPathLoss → DeadlinePower → SINR → Capacity → Airtime → Deadline
inputs: ('transmission', 'link', 'sender', 'receiver', 'size_bits', 'group', 'noise_power')
outputs: ('h', 'power', 'active', 'sinr', 'num_symbols', 'latency', 'energy', 'success')


PipelineBackend checks the wiring when it is built. Every input a block needs is either one of the step’s inputs (transmission, link, size_bits, …), the constant noise_power, or given by a block before it.
A check against eq. 10 by hand: a state sent from 100 m in line of sight, through the pipeline.

def message(sender, receiver, size_bits, k, deadline=D_TH):
    return Message(sender, receiver, None, size_bits=size_bits, metadata={'control': k, 'deadline': deadline})

def rows(messages):
    return [(Transmission(m, m.sender, m.receiver, 0.0), TOPOLOGY.get_link(m.sender, m.receiver)) for m in messages]

pl = UAVPathLoss(BS, ALTITUDE, FC_GHZ)
assert pl.p_los(10.0) == 1.0 and 0 < pl.p_los(300.0) < 1
backend.set_positions({'uav': BS + [100.0, 0.0]})                     # p_LOS = 0.79: draw until a round is in LOS
backend.reset(seed=0)
k = next(k for k in range(100) if (state := backend.pipeline(**step_inputs(rows([message('uav', 'bs', B_STATE, k)])),
                                                             noise_power=NOISE_W))['h'][0, 0] ** 2 > 10 ** (-8.5))
L = pl.path_loss_db(math.hypot(100.0, ALTITUDE), los=True)
expected = B_STATE / (W * math.log2(1 + P_DL * 10 ** (-L / 10) / NOISE_W))
assert abs(state['latency'][0] - expected) < 1 / W and state['success'][0]
print(f'L = {L:.1f} dB, SNR = {10 * math.log10(state["sinr"][0, 0]):.1f} dB, the state takes {1e3 * expected:.2f} ms')

L = 80.3 dB, SNR = -5.4 dB, the state takes 0.43 ms
crumbs: Remote UAV control, built from blocks

title: Remote UAV control, built from blocks
text:
The link along the way
How often a round completes (the state and the reply both arrive within D_th) depends on how far the UAV is from the BS and on what the BS sends back. With the pipeline alone, without a network or a UAV: 400 rounds at each distance, each state sent in one call of the blocks, then the replies with the time each has left. The replies use the same rounds, and so the same draws of line of sight.

def completes(power_control, distance, n=400, seed=0):
    "Share of n rounds at `distance` (m, horizontal) whose state and reply both arrive in time, per kind of reply."
    backend = PipelineBackend(radio(power_control), noise_power=NOISE_W)
    backend.reset(seed=seed)
    backend.set_positions({'uav': BS + [distance, 0.0]})
    states = backend.transmit_all(rows([message('uav', 'bs', B_STATE, k) for k in range(n)]))
    out = {}
    for kind, size in (('action', B_ACTION), ('model', B_MODEL)):
        replies = [message('bs', 'uav', size, k, D_TH - r.latency) for k, r in enumerate(states) if r.success]
        out[kind] = sum(r.success for r in backend.transmit_all(rows(replies))) / n
    return out

DISTANCES = np.arange(0, 601, 20)
curves = {(pc, kind): [] for pc in ('PC', 'no PC') for kind in ('action', 'model')}
for pc, make in (('PC', lambda: DeadlinePower(P_UL_MAX)), ('no PC', FixedPower)):
    for d in DISTANCES:
        for kind, share in completes(make(), d).items():
            curves[pc, kind].append(share)
p_los = [UAVPathLoss(BS, ALTITUDE, FC_GHZ).p_los(d) for d in DISTANCES]


colors = {'action': '#2a78d6', 'model': '#eb6834'}                  # categorical slots 1 and 2
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.8))
for (pc, kind), y in curves.items():
    ax.plot(DISTANCES, 100 * np.array(y), '-' if pc == 'PC' else '--', color=colors[kind], lw=2,
            label=f'{kind} ({b * M_WEIGHTS if kind == "model" else 2 * b} bits), {"with" if pc == "PC" else "without"} power control')
ax.plot(DISTANCES, 100 * np.array(p_los), ':', color='#6b6a63', lw=1.5, label='line of sight (eq. 12)')
ax.axvline(np.linalg.norm(BS), color='#6b6a63', lw=0.8)
ax.annotate('the destination', (np.linalg.norm(BS), 5), xytext=(4, 0), textcoords='offset points', fontsize=9)
ax.set(xlabel='horizontal distance from the BS (m)', ylabel='rounds completed (%)', ylim=(0, 102),
       title='Rounds whose state and reply arrive within D_th = 2 s')
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
for side in ('top', 'right'):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc='lower left')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









An action gets through wherever the state does. At 160 bits it needs little rate, and a round fails only once the state itself takes most of the 2 s. In non-line of sight, that is beyond about 260 m without power control and 280 m with it.
The controller needs much more. At 4320 bits (27× an action), it misses the deadline in non-line of sight from about 140 m. Eq. 13’s 3 dB boost moves that to about 190 m, just past the destination (180 m).
Beyond those distances, a round completes only in line of sight, which eq. 12 makes rarer with distance.
crumbs: Remote UAV control, built from blocks

title: Remote UAV control, built from blocks
text:
The controller
The UAV’s state is s = [r, v], and it moves as eq. 3: ds = (As + B(a + c₀v_o)) dt + G dW. The quadratic part of eq. 1’s cost is c₁‖r‖² + c₂‖v‖² + c₃‖a‖², whose HJB solution is ψ = sᵀPs, with P solving the Riccati equation and a = −Ks − c₀v_o (K = Bᵀ P / c₃, as eq. 6). The BS starts from P = 0 and takes one step of the Riccati equation per state it receives, which is value iteration with a horizon 0.1 s longer per update. The paper’s model starts from w = 0 (a = 0); this one starts by only cancelling the mean wind.
After 50 updates (the paper’s Dn_th), it is the LQR to within 1%:

A = np.block([[np.zeros((2, 2)), np.eye(2)], [np.zeros((2, 2)), -C0 * np.eye(2)]])
B = np.vstack([np.zeros((2, 2)), np.eye(2)])
Q, R = np.diag([C1, C1, C2, C2]), C3 * np.eye(2)

def train(P, step=0.1):
    "One update of the BS's controller: a step of the Riccati equation (value iteration)."
    return P + step * (A.T @ P + P @ A - P @ B @ np.linalg.solve(R, B.T @ P) + Q)

def model(P):
    "The weights the BS uploads: the feedback gain K."
    return np.linalg.solve(R, B.T @ P)

def act(K, s):
    "The action of the controller K at state s (eq. 6), at most A_MAX."
    a = -K @ s - C0 * V_O
    return a * min(1.0, A_MAX / np.linalg.norm(a))

P = np.zeros((4, 4))
error = []
for n in range(100):
    P = train(P)
    error.append(np.abs(model(P) - model(solve_continuous_are(A, B, Q, R))).max() / model(solve_continuous_are(A, B, Q, R)).max())
assert error[49] < 0.01 and error[9] > 0.3
print(f'after 10 updates: {100 * error[9]:.0f}% off; after 50: {100 * error[49]:.2f}%')

after 10 updates: 35% off; after 50: 0.00%
crumbs: Remote UAV control, built from blocks

title: Remote UAV control, built from blocks
text:
The rounds
Algorithms 1–3, around a Network with this pipeline as its backend. In round k:

At t_o,k the UAV sends its state (4b bits). If it arrives within D_th, after D_DL:
the BS updates its controller and, at t_o,k + D_DL, sends an action or the controller, with D_th − D_DL left. The action is computed from the state the BS received, which is D_DL old.
The UAV acts with the most recent action it received, held until the next one, or with the most recent controller it received, applied to its current state every Δt.
The next round starts when the reply arrives, or at D_th if something was lost, on the grid of Δt.

oHJB switches to the controller when it has received Dn_th states and the mean delay of the last N received states exceeds αD_th, and stays with it, as the paper’s text and Fig. 2 describe. Algorithm 3’s line 5 says “Dn ≥ Dn_th or D̄ ≤ αD_th” for actions, which contradicts the text. Dn and Up count the received states and the received replies.

RULES = {
    'aHJB': lambda dn, delay: 'action',
    'mHJB': lambda dn, delay: 'model',
    'oHJB': lambda dn, delay: 'model' if dn >= DN_TH and delay > ALPHA * D_TH else 'action',
}

def fly(rule, power_control, seed, bs=BS, t_max=600.0):
    "One mission from the BS to the origin: travel time T (inf: not reached), motion energy E(T), and the rounds."
    backend = PipelineBackend(radio(power_control, bs), noise_power=NOISE_W)
    net = Network([Node('uav'), Node('bs')], TOPOLOGY, IdealProtocol(), backend)
    net.reset(seed=seed)
    wind = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    s, t, k, P = np.r_[bs, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0, 0, np.zeros((4, 4))
    held, controller, arriving = np.zeros(2), None, deque()       # what the UAV acts with; replies on their way
    dn, up, delays, switched, energy, log = 0, 0, deque(maxlen=N_AVG), None, 0.0, []
    while t < t_max and not (np.linalg.norm(s[:2]) <= R_TH and np.linalg.norm(s[2:]) <= V_TH):
        backend.set_positions({'uav': s[:2].copy()})
        net.send(Message('uav', 'bs', s.copy(), size_bits=B_STATE, metadata={'control': k, 'deadline': D_TH}))
        [state] = net.step_to(t)
        end = t + D_TH
        if state.success:                                         # the BS has the state, D_DL after t_o,k
            dn += 1
            delays.append(state.latency)
            P = train(P)
            kind = 'model' if switched is not None else RULES[rule](dn, np.mean(delays))
            if kind == 'model' and switched is None:
                switched = t
            content = act(model(P), state.payload) if kind == 'action' else model(P)
            net.send(Message('bs', 'uav', content, size_bits=B_ACTION if kind == 'action' else B_MODEL,
                             metadata={'control': k, 'deadline': D_TH - state.latency}), at=t + state.latency)
            [reply] = net.step_to(t + state.latency)
            if reply.success:
                up += 1
                end = t + state.latency + reply.latency
                arriving.append((end, kind, reply.payload))
        steps = max(1, math.ceil((end - t) / DT - 1e-9))
        for i in range(steps):                                    # the UAV flies until the next round
            while arriving and arriving[0][0] <= t + i * DT + 1e-9:
                _, kind, content = arriving.popleft()
                held, controller = (content, None) if kind == 'action' else (held, content)
            a = act(controller, s) if controller is not None else held
            energy += (C2 * s[2:] @ s[2:] + C3 * a @ a) * DT
            s = s + np.r_[s[2:], -C0 * s[2:] + a + C0 * V_O] * DT + np.r_[0, 0, V_NOISE * math.sqrt(DT) * wind.standard_normal(2)]
        log.append((t, s[0], s[1], dn, up))
        t, k = t + steps * DT, k + 1
    reached = np.linalg.norm(s[:2]) <= R_TH and np.linalg.norm(s[2:]) <= V_TH
    return dict(T=t if reached else math.inf, E=energy, dn=dn, up=up, switched=switched if rule == 'oHJB' else None,
                comm=net.metrics.summary().total_energy, log=np.array(log))

At the paper’s distance
Each method with and without the power boost, over 8 missions (seeds: the wind and the line of sight):

SEEDS = range(8)

    ax1.set(xlabel='x (m)', ylabel='y (m)', title=f'Trajectories ({title}, seed {seed})', aspect='equal')
    ax2.set(xlabel='t (s)', ylabel='states received, Dn(t)', title='Training samples (dot: oHJB switches)')
    for ax in (ax1, ax2):
        ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
        for side in ('top', 'right'):
            ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
        ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)

show(runs, BS, "the paper's distance")









All three methods reach the destination, with or without power control. Within 180 m, the link serves all of them.
mHJB is the fastest: 41.6 s, against 48.2 s for aHJB and 46.3 s for oHJB. With the controller on board, the UAV acts on its current state every 0.1 s. An action is computed from the state at the start of the round and held until the next one arrives, so near the destination the UAV corrects late and takes longer to settle.
More training samples buy nothing here. aHJB receives the most states (317, against 216 for mHJB). But the stand-in controller is fully trained after 50 of them, in the first 5 s, while the UAV is close to the BS and every reply takes under 0.1 s. That removes the paper’s reason to send actions first. Its HJB NN trains slowly, so there the extra samples matter.
Power control matters only for mHJB, and little. It boosts the controller’s uploads in non-line of sight beyond 140 m. A lost upload leaves the UAV with the previous controller, already trained, so the travel time barely changes (41.6 s against 41.2 s), while the radio energy goes from 3.9 J to 6.2 J. Actions never need the boost within 180 m.
oHJB switches at about 35 s (the median), once its last five states took 0.4 s on average. That happens in non-line of sight, far out.

title: Remote UAV control, built from blocks
text:
Farther from the base station
The same mission with the BS (and the start) 2× and 3× as far from the destination, 361 m and 541 m. Power control is on: beyond about 300 m, a round in non-line of sight loses the state itself, before the BS could boost anything (the figure above).

far = {scale: table(BS * scale, {'PC': POWER['PC']}) for scale in (2, 3)}

                reached   T (s)    E(T)    Dn    Up  radio (J)  switch (s)
aHJB, PC             0%     inf   268.3   462   458      56.85         nan
mHJB, PC           100%    63.5    48.2   218   212       7.26         nan
oHJB, PC           100%    61.8    48.2   276   272       4.79        32.6
                reached   T (s)    E(T)    Dn    Up  radio (J)  switch (s)
aHJB, PC             0%     inf   406.0   358   358      57.29         nan
mHJB, PC           100%    81.4    74.8   220   214       8.97         nan
oHJB, PC           100%    79.9    74.8   278   274       6.59        32.7



show(far[2], 2 * BS, '2× as far')









aHJB never arrives. Beyond 300 m, a round in non-line of sight loses the state, and the UAV holds its last action for the whole 2 s, often for several rounds in a row. A saturated action held that long overshoots, which takes the UAV farther from the BS, where more rounds are lost. In the figure, it circles the destination, as far as 270 m from it, until the 600 s limit. This is the failure the paper reports for aHJB.
mHJB and oHJB arrive every time, within 2.5% of each other’s travel time: 63.5 s and 61.8 s at 2×, 81.4 s and 79.9 s at 3×. A UAV that runs its controller loses nothing when a round is lost.
oHJB uses about a third less radio energy than mHJB: 4.8 J against 7.3 J at 2×, and 6.6 J against 9.0 J at 3×. Near the BS, actions do as well as the controller at 1/27 of the size. oHJB switches at about 33 s, once the rounds slow down.

Against the paper. The communication model gives the paper’s trade-off: actions are cheap and work while the link holds, and only a controller on board survives losing it. oHJB arrives whenever mHJB does. Its travel time is within 2.5% of mHJB’s far from the BS and 11% longer at the paper’s distance, and it uses the least radio energy of the methods that arrive far out. The paper also finds oHJB 13% faster than both, and mHJB failing without power control. Those results depend on how slowly its HJB NN trains, which the stand-in controller doesn’t reproduce. Replacing the controller is a change to the application only. The blocks and the network stay as they are.

title: Power control without channel knowledge
text:
Agents on a 9 × 9 grid send each other a 7 × 7 map of codebook tokens at every step: 49 indices into a codebook of 256, so 392 bits. The link is the communication model of C3-WM:
The transmitter does not know the current gain |h_t|², so it predicts it. The predictors compared here:
Comparing them fairly. The transmitter’s job (C3-WM’s eq. 14) is to reach the target SNR with as little power as possible. A predictor that underestimates gains reaches the target more often, but spends more power. So each predictor is run with a margin m (ρ = Γσ²·m/ĝ), swept. It is judged by the mean power it needs, relative to perfect CSI’s, to reach the target on 90%, 95% or 99% of the transmissions that perfect CSI can serve within ρ_max. Links it misses count as failures, and power spent on links that cannot be served counts as cost.
(Counting lost tokens within a fixed power budget would judge something else: under a total budget, abandoning weak links and favouring strong ones loses fewer tokens than reaching the target on every link. That metric mixes the quality of the prediction with the choice of policy.)
import math

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from comm_core import *

title: Power control without channel knowledge
text:
The channel map
The channel between every pair of grid cells, as a ray tracer gives it. Here it’s a room with a line-of-sight path and a reflection off each of the 4 walls, at 2.4 GHz. With Sionna RT, use paths.cfr(..., normalize=False) and RayTracedFading.from_files.

C, F = 299_792_458.0, 2.4e9
SIZE, HEIGHT = 9, 0.5
cells = [(x, y) for x in range(SIZE) for y in range(SIZE)]
WALLS = [(0, -0.5, -0.6), (0, SIZE - 0.5, -0.6), (1, -0.5, -0.5), (1, SIZE - 0.5, -0.5)]   # (axis, coordinate, reflection)

def channel(tx, rx):
    "Line of sight + one reflection off each wall (image method)."
    tx, rx = np.array([*tx, HEIGHT]), np.array([*rx, HEIGHT])
    h = 0j
    for source, gain in [(tx, 1.0)] + [(tx * np.where(np.arange(3) == a, -1, 1) + 2 * c * (np.arange(3) == a), g) for a, c, g in WALLS]:
        L = np.linalg.norm(rx - source)
        h += gain * C / F / (4 * np.pi * L) * np.exp(-2j * np.pi * F * L / C)
    return h

H = np.array([[channel(tx, rx) if tx != rx else 0 for tx in cells] for rx in cells])   # H[rx, tx]
fading = RayTracedFading(H, cells)
print(f'{len(cells)} cells; path gain between cells: {10 * np.log10(np.abs(H[H != 0]) ** 2).min():.0f} to '
      f'{10 * np.log10(np.abs(H[H != 0]) ** 2).max():.0f} dB')

81 cells; path gain between cells: -91 to -39 dB

title: Power control without channel knowledge
Power control without channel knowledge
text:
Fitting the history predictors
The training set (C3-WM’s D_channel) holds the gain of every directed link at every step of recorded episodes. gain_windows turns it into (last 4 gains → next gain) pairs, and fit_gain_predictor fits the linear predictors. The map predictors need no training.

gain = lambda tx, rx: fading.gain_between(tx, rx)
LINKS = [(s, r) for s in AGENTS for r in AGENTS if s != r]

def link_gains(episode):
    return {(s, r): [gain(pos[s], pos[r]) for pos, _ in episode] for s, r in LINKS}

training = [g for seed in range(300) for g in link_gains(walks(seed)).values()]
psi_lin = fit_gain_predictor(training, history=HISTORY)                   # C3-WM's eq. 24
psi_db = fit_gain_predictor(training, history=HISTORY, domain='db')

title: Power control without channel knowledge
text:
The comparison
On test episodes, each predictor’s estimate is computed for every directed link at every step, from what the transmitter would know then. For any margin, the power, whether it is sent, and whether the SNR reaches the target then follow directly.

db = lambda g: 10 * np.log10(np.maximum(g, 1e-30))
erfc = np.vectorize(math.erfc)
SNR_TARGET, NOISE_W, MAX_POWER_W = 10 ** 0.7, 10 ** ((-94 - 30) / 10), 2e-5          # Γ = 7 dB, σ² = -94 dBm, ρ_max = 20 µW
estimates = {k: [] for k in ('last gain', 'linear on |h|²', 'linear in dB', "map, receiver's last cell", 'map, robust', 'perfect CSI')}
truth = []
for seed in range(10_000, 10_040):
    episode = walks(seed)
    for s, r in LINKS:
        g = [gain(pos[s], pos[r]) for pos, _ in episode]
        for t in range(HISTORY, STEPS):
            past = np.array(g[t - HISTORY:t][::-1])                       # most recent first
            (pos, _), (pos_before, head_before) = episode[t], episode[t - 1]
            truth.append(g[t])
            estimates['last gain'].append(past[0])
            estimates['linear on |h|²'].append(max(psi_lin(past), 0.0))
            estimates['linear in dB'].append(psi_db(past))
            estimates["map, receiver's last cell"].append(gain(pos[s], pos_before[r]))
            near = [c for c in reachable(pos_before[r], head_before[r]) if c in fading.index]
            estimates['map, robust'].append(min(gain(pos[s], c) for c in ([c for c in near if c != pos[s]] or near)))
            estimates['perfect CSI'].append(g[t])
truth = np.array(truth)
estimates = {k: np.array(v) for k, v in estimates.items()}

servable = SNR_TARGET * NOISE_W / truth <= MAX_POWER_W            # perfect CSI can serve these
perfect_power = np.where(servable, SNR_TARGET * NOISE_W / truth, 0.0).mean()

def outcome(estimate, margin_db):
    "(share of the servable transmissions reaching the target, mean power relative to perfect CSI's) at a margin."
    power = SNR_TARGET * NOISE_W * 10 ** (margin_db / 10) / np.maximum(estimate, 1e-30)
    sent = power <= MAX_POWER_W
    reached = sent & (power * truth / NOISE_W >= SNR_TARGET * (1 - 1e-9))
    return reached[servable].mean(), np.where(sent, power, 0.0).mean() / perfect_power

margins = np.arange(-6, 30.01, 0.1)
curves = {k: np.array([outcome(e, m) for m in margins]) for k, e in estimates.items()}

def power_for(k, share):
    "Least relative power at which predictor k reaches the target on `share` of the servable transmissions."
    ok = curves[k][:, 0] >= share
    return curves[k][ok, 1].min() if ok.any() else np.inf

print(f"{'':26s} {'error (dB): mean':>16s} {'spread':>7s} | power to reach Γ on 90 / 95 / 99% (× perfect CSI)")
for k, e in estimates.items():
    err = db(e) - db(truth)
    err = err[np.isfinite(err)]                                    # same cell: no error to measure
    print(f'{k:26s} {err.mean():+16.1f} {err.std():7.1f} | ' +
          '  '.join(f'{power_for(k, q):5.1f}' if np.isfinite(power_for(k, q)) else '  -  ' for q in (0.9, 0.95, 0.99)))

                           error (dB): mean  spread | power to reach Γ on 90 / 95 / 99% (× perfect CSI)
last gain                              -0.0     4.1 |   1.9    -      -  
linear on |h|²                         +1.8     4.4 |   1.4    2.7    -  
linear in dB                           +0.0     3.9 |   1.5    -      -  
map, receiver's last cell              -0.0     3.0 |   1.0    -      -  
map, robust                            -2.1     3.7 |   1.4    1.4    1.4
perfect CSI                            +0.0     0.0 |   1.0    1.0    1.0



fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.6))
style = {'last gain': ':', 'linear on |h|²': '--', 'linear in dB': '-', "map, receiver's last cell": '-.', 'map, robust': '-'}
powers = np.geomspace(0.5, 10, 300)
for k, ls in style.items():
    best = [curves[k][curves[k][:, 1] <= p, 0].max() if (curves[k][:, 1] <= p).any() else np.nan for p in powers]
    ax.plot(powers, 100 * np.array(best), ls, lw=2.4 if k == 'map, robust' else 1.5, label=k)
ax.plot(1, 100, 'k*', ms=14, label='perfect CSI')
ax.set(xscale='log', ylim=(50, 101), xlabel='mean power, relative to perfect CSI', ylabel='target SNR reached (%)',
       title='Servable transmissions reaching the target, against the power spent')
ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which='both'); ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc='lower right')
plt.tight_layout()

title: Power control without channel knowledge
text:
The same through a network
The analysis above, checked by running comm-core’s power controls for real, one operating point each. Each predictor runs with the margin at which it reaches the target on 90% of the servable transmissions, with the least power, through a LinkLevelChannel: every bit, with the gain histories and position reports kept by the power controls themselves.

def margin_at(k, share=0.9):
    "The margin at which predictor k reaches the target on `share` of the servable transmissions with the least power."
    ok = curves[k][:, 0] >= share
    return margins[ok][np.argmin(curves[k][ok, 1])]

margin_for = {k: margin_at(k) for k in style}
margin_for['perfect CSI'] = 0.0
heads = {}

def power_control(name, m):
    if name == 'perfect CSI':
        return ChannelInversion(7.0, max_power=MAX_POWER_W)
    if name.startswith('map'):
        return MapChannelInversion(fading, reachable=reachable if name == 'map, robust' else None, states=lambda: heads,
                                   target_snr_db=7.0, max_power=MAX_POWER_W, margin_db=m, fallback=FixedPower(MAX_POWER_W / 2))
    predictor = {'last gain': lambda past: past[0], 'linear on |h|²': psi_lin, 'linear in dB': psi_db}[name]
    return PredictedChannelInversion(predictor, 1 if name == 'last gain' else HISTORY, 7.0, MAX_POWER_W,
                                     fallback_power=MAX_POWER_W / 2, margin_db=m)

def simulate(name, episodes=range(10_000, 10_040)):
    radio = LinkLevelChannel(codec=IndexCodec(256), modulation=BPSK(), fading=fading,
                             power_control=power_control(name, margin_for[name]), noise_power=NOISE_W)
    net = Network([Node(a) for a in AGENTS], FullMeshTopology(AGENTS), IdealProtocol(), AnalyticalBackend(radio))
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    reached, power = [], []
    for seed in episodes:
        episode = walks(seed)
        net.reset(seed)
        for t, (pos, head) in enumerate(episode):
            radio.set_positions(pos)
            heads.clear(); heads.update(head)
            tokens = {a: rng.integers(0, 256, 49) for a in AGENTS}
            for s, r in LINKS:
                net.send(Message(s, r, payload=tokens[s], type='tokens'))
            for res in net.step():
                if t < HISTORY or math.isinf(res.snr_db):          # as in the analysis: from step 4 on
                    continue
                g = 10 ** (res.metadata['channel_gain_db'] / 10)
                power.append(res.metadata['tx_power'])
                if SNR_TARGET * NOISE_W / g <= MAX_POWER_W:                    # servable
                    reached.append(res.success and res.snr_db >= 7.0 - 1e-9)
    return np.mean(reached), np.mean(power) / perfect_power

print(f"{'':26s} {'margin':>8s} {'simulated: reached':>19s} {'power':>6s} | {'analysis: reached':>18s} {'power':>6s}")
for name in list(style) + ['perfect CSI']:
    sim_reached, sim_power = simulate(name)
    ana_reached, ana_power = outcome(estimates[name], margin_for[name])
    print(f'{name:26s} {margin_for[name]:+6.1f}dB {100 * sim_reached:18.1f}% {sim_power:5.2f}x | {100 * ana_reached:17.1f}% {ana_power:5.2f}x')

                             margin  simulated: reached  power |  analysis: reached  power
last gain                    +3.9dB               90.1%  1.91x |              90.1%  1.91x
linear on |h|²               +5.4dB               90.0%  1.42x |              90.0%  1.42x
linear in dB                 +3.1dB               90.0%  1.48x |              90.0%  1.48x
map, receiver's last cell    -0.0dB               90.1%  1.00x |              90.0%  1.00x
map, robust                  +0.5dB               98.3%  1.43x |              98.3%  1.43x
perfect CSI                  +0.0dB              100.0%  1.00x |             100.0%  1.00x



History alone can’t make the target reliable. Last step’s gain, a linear fit on |h|² (C3-WM’s) or in dB: each reaches the target 90% of the time with a margin, but not 95% or 99% within the power budget. Their errors have too wide a spread (several dB) for any margin to cover. Agents move a whole cell, many wavelengths, between steps, so a link’s past says little about its next gain.
Fitted on |h|², the predictor is biased (it overestimates weak links) and needs a large margin. In dB, it is unbiased and needs less.
The map gives the transmitter what the history lacks. The receiver’s last reported cell alone predicts with less spread. With its reported heading as well, the robust lookup takes the weakest cell the receiver can have reached. It never overestimates, so it reaches the target on nearly every servable transmission, at a fixed extra power over perfect CSI.
The cost is a few bits of position and heading in each message, and a ray-traced map of the area, which C3-WM computes anyway.
Through a network (MapChannelInversion, PredictedChannelInversion), the simulation agrees with the analysis. Small differences come from the first steps of each episode, where the power controls fall back to a fixed power.


assert np.isfinite(power_for('map, robust', 0.99))
assert all(power_for(k, 0.99) == np.inf for k in ('last gain', 'linear on |h|²', 'linear in dB'))
assert power_for('map, robust', 0.95) < min(power_for(k, 0.95) for k in ('last gain', 'linear on |h|²', 'linear in dB'))

title: Sionna PHY
text:
The link level of 5G NR with Sionna PHY: every bit of every transmission, coded and decoded the way an NR receiver does it.

The payload becomes bits (a Codec, e.g. IndexCodec for codebook indices).
Coding: the bits become an NR transport block, with a CRC, LDPC coding and rate matching (TBEncoder), at the MCS of the transmission.
Modulation: QAM (Mapper).
The channel: the symbols go out on resource elements, filling the subcarriers in turn. Each sees the channel of its subcarrier: y = h_k √P x + n, where the noise includes any interference.
The receiver: it equalizes each resource element (one tap, knowing h_k), computes soft bits (Demapper, LLRs), and decodes the LDPC code (TBDecoder).

The CRC decides delivery, as in a real receiver: a transport block that fails its CRC is lost.
SionnaLink is this chain as a block (see block), and SionnaLinkChannel is the RadioChannel whose receiver it is, like SystemLevelChannel and LinkLevelChannel. It takes the same fadings (e.g. RayTracedPathsFading with subcarriers), power control, InterferenceBackend and protocols. It needs Sionna 2 (PyTorch): pip install 'comm-core[sionna]'.
The MCS: a fixed mcs_index, or link adaptation (the default). Link adaptation picks the highest MCS that Sionna SYS (SionnaErrorModel) predicts to meet bler_target at the transmission’s SINR. The transmitter is assumed to know the channel.
The results add mcs, resource_elements, tb_size (the NR transport block, padded to an allowed size) and bit_errors to their metadata. error_rate is the bit error rate of the decoded payload.
MCSs: those with code rates below 1/5 (MCS 0–2 of table 1) are not available. Sionna’s LDPC encoder doesn’t support them (NR reaches them by repetition), so link adaptation chooses from the others.
Cost: LDPC decoding is heavy, around 25 ms per 1000-bit message on a CPU, much less on a GPU. Use it to check the system level (SionnaErrorModel), or where the bits themselves matter. For training, SystemLevelChannel with SionnaErrorModel is the fast equivalent.

Tests
These need Sionna, so they are flagged (#| sionna): nbdev_test --flags sionna runs them.
The link level against the system level. At MCS 10, 1000-bit messages are sent over a flat channel. The fraction lost (the transport block error rate, TBLER) is compared with what SionnaErrorModel predicts. The PHY abstraction should place the error-rate curve within about a dB of the simulation.

from comm_core.link import UniformQuantizer
from comm_core.propagation import NoFading
from comm_core.power_control import ChannelInversion


def send_all(channel, payloads, link=Link('a', 'b')):
    pairs = [(Transmission(message=Message('a', 'b', p), sender='a', receiver='b', start_time=0.0), link) for p in payloads]
    return channel.transmit_batch(pairs)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
codec = UniformQuantizer(bits=8, low=0, high=1)                        # 125 numbers: 1000 bits
payloads = [rng.uniform(0, 1, 125) for _ in range(200)]
model = SionnaErrorModel(mcs_index=10)
print(' SINR   simulated TBLER, 20 / 50 decoder iterations   SYS predicted')
for snr_db in (2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0):
    lost = []
    for iterations in (20, 50):
        channel = SionnaLinkChannel(codec=codec, noise_power=10 ** (-snr_db / 10), mcs_index=10, num_bp_iter=iterations, seed=1)
        lost.append(1 - np.mean([r.success for r in send_all(channel, payloads)]))
    predicted = model([np.array([10 ** (snr_db / 10)])], np.array([1000]))[0][0]
    print(f'{snr_db:4.1f} dB {lost[0]:21.3f} / {lost[1]:.3f} {predicted:20.3f}')
    if predicted <= 0.01:
        assert lost[1] <= 0.2
    if predicted >= 0.99:
        assert lost[1] >= 0.8

 4.5 dB                 0.000 / 0.000                0.001
